data.curve_reference: Offsets in dB relative to the Harman in-ear 2019 target (Olive et al.). IEMs are compared against that target plus these offsets.

assumptions.basis: Harman listener classes: 64% prefer the target, 15% want 4-6 dB more bass, 21% about 2 dB less (Olive 2022). That mixture alone has an SD of about 2.1 dB; within-class spread is added.
Demographic groups differ by about 2 dB in preferred treble (Olive & Welti 2015).
Listeners strongly rejected both the 2-4 kHz emphasis of diffuse-field targets and too little energy there (Olive et al. 2013); variation in the midrange is assumed smaller than in bass.
No preference data; set like treble. Couplers are unreliable above 10 kHz anyway.
Conservative minimum reliability of single-item self-report measures (Wanous, Reichers & Hudy 1997). Borrowed from a neighbouring field, not measured for audio questions.
An answer inferred from a neighbouring question (e.g. air from treble) keeps half the reliability of a direct one.

Correlation between a library's spectral balance and the listener's preferred balance. No study has measured it (research.md section 3). The sign follows the content-matching hypothesis; the magnitude makes a large library exactly as informative as one direct answer (rho^2 = answer reliability).

summary: Warmth: leaning warm (+1.3 dB vs the reference), from your music.
Vocal presence: leaning laid-back (-0.7 dB vs the reference), from your music.
Treble: leaning smooth (-1.0 dB vs the reference), from your music.

descriptors.label: Dynamics
